prime.problem: The bigram model predicts each next character from the current character alone. Everything earlier in the chunk is sitting right there in the tensor, but no token can see it, so training stalls around val loss 2.49.
prime.fits: This opens the lecture's self-attention section. It builds on the batches-of-chunks card, where position t of a chunk is a training example whose target is the character at t + 1, and on the bigram baseline it tries to beat.
expect: the (B, T, C) axes: batch, time, channels
causal mixing: position t uses positions 0…t only
why equal weights and lost order make it weak
prime.goal: Write the xbow double loop, compute any row by hand, say why it must stop at position t, and name the two things it throws away.

attend: Why must token t's mix stop at position t, when the later characters of the chunk are right there in the same tensor?
What happens to the current token's own share of xbow[b,t] as t grows, and what does that do to the last position?
Which facts about the past survive averaging, and which (order, which token said what) are destroyed?
Why does the loop run over b as well as t, and could editing sequence 0 ever change sequence 1's xbow?
In the formula, which single factor would have to become learned and unequal to turn this into attention?

must: In next-character training, position t's target is the character at t + 1 of the same chunk → any mix that includes positions after t leaks the answer → the slice x[b,:t+1] stops at t → the same model still works at generation time, when no future exists

Every token in the past gets the same weight 1/(t + 1) → the current token's own share falls to 1/8 at t = 7 → xbow[0,7] = [−0.0341, 0.1332] barely resembles x[0,7] = [−0.9211, 1.5433] → the one earlier token that matters is blurred with all the rest

A mean is a sum divided by a count, and a sum ignores order → reordering tokens 0…t gives the same xbow[b,t] (a "bag of words") → order has to come back from position embeddings, and relevance from learned weights
elevated: The double loop makes one small torch call per (b, t) pair → 32 calls in the toy, 64 × 256 = 16,384 at gpt.py's batch and block size → the next card replaces the whole loop with one triangular matrix multiply that gives the same numbers
reference: torch.mean(xprev, 0): mean over dim 0 of the (t+1, C) slice, i.e. over time
xbow = "x bag of words"; Karpathy's comment says (t,C) but the slice has t + 1 rows

compress.prompt: From memory, write the xbow rule as a formula, then explain in 3–4 sentences why it stops at position t and what two kinds of information it loses.
checklist: stopping at t keeps it causal: the target for t sits at t + 1
each sequence in the batch is averaged separately
equal weights: every past token gets the same say, so the useful one is diluted
order is lost: any shuffle of the past gives the same mean

retrieve.q: Nothing in xbow is learned. Explain in what sense it still counts as tokens "talking" to each other, and why that is progress over the bigram model.
answer: after averaging, token t's vector contains information from tokens 0…t
a layer that reads xbow[b,t] can therefore use context, not only the current character
the bigram model reads a single row and cannot use anything earlier, however long it trains

retrieve.q: Walk through computing xbow[0,2] from the first three rows of x[0]: [0.1808, −0.0700], [−0.3596, −0.9152], [0.6258, 0.0255].
answer: slice x[0,:3], a (3, 2) tensor
sum down the time axis: [0.4469, −0.9597] (at full precision)
rows 3–7 never enter the calculation

retrieve.q: Instead of averaging, a colleague wants to concatenate every past vector so nothing is lost. What does that buy, and why doesn't the lecture do it?
answer: buys: exact values and their order are kept
cost: the size grows with t (2 numbers at t = 0, 16 at t = 7 in the toy; 256 × 384 = 98,304 at gpt.py's size)
the next layer needs a fixed input size, so a fixed-size summary is needed
a weighted sum keeps the fixed size; attention later makes the weights smart

retrieve.q: Suppose the inner slice were x[b,:] instead of x[b,:t+1]. What goes wrong in training, and what goes wrong in generation?
answer: every row becomes the whole-chunk mean ([−0.0341, 0.1332] for sequence 0)
training: position t's input contains the character it must predict, so the loss rewards reading the answer
generation: the future doesn't exist yet, so the model meets inputs unlike anything it trained on

compare.q: Both give each position one fixed-size vector to predict from. What is fundamentally different about what that vector can contain, and how does each one fail?
answer: bigram: the vector is looked up from the current character only
average: the vector mixes the current character with all earlier ones
bigram fails by ignoring context entirely (stuck near val 2.49)
average fails by weighting every past token equally and forgetting order

compare.q: Both output a weighted mix of earlier tokens. Which design choice separates them, and when would the plain average be good enough?
answer: average: weights fixed at 1/(t + 1), the same for every sequence
attention: weights from query·key scores, so they depend on the tokens' contents
the average is fine when every past item is about equally useful and order doesn't matter (e.g. a simple bag-of-words summary)
for next-character prediction the nearby, specific characters matter, so equal weights are too blunt

predict.q: In sequence 0, shuffle the first three tokens so the order becomes x[0,2], x[0,0], x[0,1], and leave the rest alone. Which rows of xbow[0] change: all of them, rows 0–2, or only rows 0–1?
predict.answer: Only rows 0 and 1. Row 0 becomes the old x[0,2] = [0.6258, 0.0255] and row 1 becomes [0.4033, −0.0222]. Rows 2–7 are identical (torch.allclose is True), because from row 2 on each mean includes all three shuffled tokens, and a sum doesn't care about order. The model can't tell "ab" from "ba" once both are in the past, which is why position embeddings come in a few cards later.

apply.task: Replace the double loop in labs/average-the-past.py with a loop-free version: a running sum along the time axis, divided by 1, 2, …, 8. Use x.cumsum(1) and torch.arange(1, T+1), reshaped so it broadcasts over (B, T, C). Compare with the loop's xbow.
apply.done: torch.allclose(xbow, xbow_fast) prints True, with a max absolute difference of about 1.19e-07 (float rounding), and you can say which axis the cumsum runs over and why.
apply.hint: The divisor must have shape (1, T, 1): one count per position, shared across the batch and the channels.
